C005.subject: The maximum amount of reliably transmissible information about AGI feasibility within 20 years
C005.object: the expected variance in compute-efficiency gains from algorithmic improvements over the next decade
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: The maximum amount of reliably transmissible information about AGI feasibility within 20 years the expected variance in compute-efficiency gains from algorithmic improvements over the next decade]

[PATH:empirical] Historical tracking of compute-efficiency gains from algorithmic improvements in AI (e.g., scaling laws literature, Hernandez & Brown 2020, Sevilla et al. 2022) — Empirical measurement of past variance in algorithmic efficiency gains provides a baseline to estimate the expected variance over the next decade, directly testing the bound on transmissible information.

[PATH:theoretical] Formal information-theoretic analysis of the relationship between algorithmic improvement uncertainty and AGI feasibility prediction — A theoretical model can derive whether the variance in compute-efficiency gains necessarily bounds the amount of reliable information about AGI feasibility, clarifying the logical structure of the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Survey of expert forecasts on algorithmic efficiency improvements and AGI timelines (e.g., AI Impacts, Metaculus, expert elicitation studies) — Aggregated expert judgments on the range of possible algorithmic gains can be compared to the variance implied by the hypothesis, providing a cross-check on whether the bound is plausible.

C006.subject: The maximum amount of reliably transmissible information about AGI feasibility within 20 years
C006.object: the irreducible uncertainty in scaling laws
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: The maximum amount of reliably transmissible information about AGI feasibility within 20 years the irreducible uncertainty in scaling laws]

[PATH:empirical] Systematic meta-analysis of scaling law prediction errors across major language model families (e.g., GPT, PaLM, LLaMA) to quantify irreducible vs. reducible uncertainty components — If the irreducible uncertainty in scaling laws is small relative to other sources of uncertainty (e.g., architectural choices, data quality), then the hypothesis that it does not constrain transmissible information about AGI feasibility would be supported. Conversely, large irreducible uncertainty would refute it.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical derivation of fundamental limits to scaling law extrapolation based on information-theoretic bounds (e.g., finite sample complexity, model capacity) and their implications for predicting emergent capabilities — This would clarify whether irreducible uncertainty is a fundamental bottleneck or merely a practical limitation, directly addressing the predicate 'is not constrained by' in the hypothesis.

C007.subject: The maximum amount of reliably transmissible information about AGI feasibility within 20 years
C007.object: the absence of a consensus formal definition of general intelligence, rather than by the lack of validated benchmarks
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: The maximum amount of reliably transmissible information about AGI feasibility within 20 years the absence of a consensus formal definition of general intelligence, rather than by the lack of validated benchmarks]

[PATH:literature] A systematic meta-analysis of existing AGI definitions in the AI literature, categorizing their operationalizability and consensus levels across major research communities (e.g., AAAI, NeurIPS, IJCAI). — This would directly assess the degree of definitional consensus, providing evidence for or against the claim that absence of definition is the primary constraint on transmitting feasibility information.

[PATH:empirical] A controlled empirical study comparing the reliability of AGI feasibility predictions made by experts when given (a) a formal definition of general intelligence vs. (b) a set of validated benchmarks without a formal definition. — This would test whether the definitional gap actually limits information transmission more than benchmark absence, by measuring inter-expert agreement and predictive accuracy under both conditions.

[PATH:theoretical] A theoretical analysis of information-theoretic bounds on transmissible knowledge about AGI feasibility, modeling the role of definitional ambiguity vs. benchmark noise as sources of uncertainty. — This could formalize whether definitional consensus is mathematically more limiting than benchmark validity for reliable information transmission, offering a principled refutation or confirmation of the hypothesis.

C008.subject: The maximum amount of reliably transmissible information about AGI feasibility within 20 years
C008.object: the lack of validated benchmarks for general intelligence
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: The maximum amount of reliably transmissible information about AGI feasibility within 20 years the lack of validated benchmarks for general intelligence]

[PATH:empirical] A longitudinal meta-analysis tracking predictive accuracy of AGI timelines against benchmark performance improvements (e.g., from ARC, MMLU, or similar) over the next 5–10 years — If benchmark saturation correlates poorly with expert forecasts of AGI feasibility, this would support the hypothesis that benchmark limitations do not bound information transmission about AGI. Conversely, strong correlation would refute it.

[PATH:theoretical] Formal information-theoretic analysis of the channel capacity of current AI evaluation frameworks for conveying AGI-relevant properties (e.g., generalization, transfer, autonomy) — This would determine whether theoretical limits on benchmark expressiveness impose an upper bound on what can be reliably communicated about AGI feasibility, directly testing the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of historical AI evaluation benchmarks and their documented relationship to subsequent AGI milestones or capability leaps — If historical benchmarks have consistently failed to predict or bound major AGI-relevant advances, this would support the hypothesis; if they have been reliable indicators, it would refute it.

evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: The maximum amount of reliably transmissible information about AGI feasibility within 20 years the unpredictability of the rate and nature of conceptual breakthroughs, even if scaling laws and benchmarks are bypassed]

[PATH:empirical] Historical analysis of conceptual breakthroughs in AI (e.g., deep learning, transformers, reinforcement learning) and their impact on feasibility forecasts, using bibliometric and citation lag data to quantify information transmission delays and prediction errors. — Directly tests whether past breakthrough rates and nature were predictable ex-ante, providing an empirical baseline for the claimed bound on transmissible information.

[PATH:theoretical] Formal modeling of the space of possible conceptual breakthroughs in AGI, using computational complexity and algorithmic information theory to derive theoretical limits on predictability from first principles (e.g., Chaitin's incompleteness, no-free-lunch theorems). — Supports or refutes the claim that unpredictability is a fundamental, not just practical, constraint on information transmission about feasibility.

[PATH:empirical] Expert elicitation and prediction market studies specifically designed to track the evolution of AGI feasibility beliefs over time, with controlled information feeds (e.g., withholding some breakthrough signals) to measure how much consensus changes with new conceptual insights. — Provides direct evidence on the rate and reliability of information transmission under varying degrees of breakthrough unpredictability, isolating the effect of conceptual novelty.
